To use pronominal verbs with “en”: s’en aller, s’en faire, s’en sortir, s’en remettre, s’en vouloir.
To use “en vouloir à quelqu’un” (to hold a grudge) and “en avoir assez / marre” (to be fed up).
To use expressions with “y”: s’y faire, s’y prendre, y tenir, y être pour quelque chose.
To conjugate these verbs in compound tenses (je m’en suis allé, je m’y suis fait).
To comfort and encourage someone: Ne t’en fais pas, tu t’en sortiras.

Thursday, 15 May 2031. Odile has been in the Croix-Rousse hospital for five days, with pneumonia. Julien comes to see her in the afternoon, with a bunch of lily of the valley and Henri-Ion in the baby carrier.
Hello, Odile. How are you feeling today?
I’m fed up with this bed. And this drip. And the soup. But I’m getting used to it. You get used to anything at my age.
I blame myself for not seeing how tired you were. I should have called Dr Martin sooner.
Don’t blame yourself. It’s not your fault. I’m the one who said nothing. I didn’t want anyone to worry about me.
The doctor says you’re doing well. Another week, and you’ll be able to go home.
Doctors always say that. I was a doctor, I know how you go about reassuring families.
Don’t worry, my dear. I’m not going just yet. I still have things to do. The lime trees in Paris and Corsica, for example. And I care about that.
You just called me “tu”. In five years you’d never done that.
It was about time, wasn’t it? At eighty you have the right to say “tu” to whoever you like. Give me that baby.
(puts Henri-Ion in her arms) He’s asleep. He fell asleep on the bus. He’ll never get over that journey.
(smiles) I’ll never get over it either. Over him. Over all of you. You know, Julien, I still can’t believe it. Five years ago I was an old lady alone with a cat. And look at me.
Look at you. With a baby in your arms and a drip.
Exactly. I’ve never been so rich.
(“en avoir assez” = to be fed up)
(“se faire à” = to get used to)
(“n’y être pour rien” = to not be at fault)
These verbs have a meaning you can’t guess from their parts. Learn them as expressions:
Je ne m’en vais pas tout de suite.
Je m’en veux de ne pas être venu.
The imperative of “s’en aller”: “Va-t’en !” (go away!), “Allez-vous-en !” (go away! — plural/polite). Negative: “Ne t’en va pas !” (don’t go!).
J’en ai assez de ce lit.
to be unable to believe it
Don’t confuse: “Je t’en veux” = I hold it against you. “Je te veux” = I want you. “En” changes the meaning completely!
Je m’y fais. / Je m’y suis faite.
Je sais comment on s’y prend.
to have nothing to do with it
“Ça y est !” = That’s it! Done it! — one of the most common spoken expressions.
Pronominal verbs take ÊTRE. The pronoun “en” or “y” goes between the reflexive pronoun and the auxiliary:
I got used to it very quickly. (feminine agreement)
She got through it. / She managed.
They blamed themselves for years. (no agreement: “se” is an indirect object)
Pronoun order: me / te / se + y + en. “Il s’en va”, “Je m’y fais”, “Il y en a”. Never “en y”.
Ne t’en fais pas. / Ne vous en faites pas.
Ce n’est pas ta faute. Tu n’y es pour rien.

I blame myself for not seeing you were tired.

On Saturday 3 May 2031, at seven in the morning, a little voice woke the whole building on rue d’Austerlitz. It wasn’t Henri-Ion, for once. It was Rose-Hélène, standing on the landing in her pyjamas, whistling. She whistled out of tune, with lots of breath and few notes, but you could recognise without any doubt the first three bars of the waltz.

She had learned on her own, in secret, for three weeks. Ever since she had heard Isabelle read Henri’s promise — every 3 May, wherever he was, he would whistle the waltz — she had been practising in her room in the evening, when she thought no one was listening. Ioana had heard her several times. She hadn’t said anything. Some surprises you have to know how to wait for.

Odile’s door opened. She was there, leaning on her stick, in her dressing gown, her hair loose. She watched the little girl whistling on the landing, and her eyes filled with tears. When Rose-Hélène had finished, very proud, Odile whistled the next three bars in turn. Then they carried on together, the old lady and the little girl, to the end of the first verse.

“Henri had made himself a promise,” Odile said, stroking Rose-Hélène’s hair. “For sixty years he never forgot it. Now you’re the one who will keep it.” Rose-Hélène nodded, very serious, as if she had just been entrusted with a secret mission. At three she had already understood that some promises are handed down like precious objects.

That day was also Hélène’s birthday — she would have been eighty-nine — and the second anniversary of her death. It was Julien and Ioana’s fourth wedding anniversary. And the next day, Radu and Lucia would celebrate their first wedding anniversary. Odile declared that May was the busiest month of the year and that she was fed up with all these anniversaries. She was lying, of course.

In the afternoon they all went to the Parc de la Tête d’Or, to the old lime tree. Odile went by taxi, then in a wheelchair, pushed by Isabelle, who had come from Paris for the weekend. She refused the wheelchair at first. Then she finally accepted, grumbling that it was only this once and that she would never get used to it.

Mr Fournier was waiting for them by the tree. The first leaves had just appeared, a very tender green. Odile asked to be brought close to the trunk. She put her hand on the bark, next to the two carved letters. She stayed like that for a long time, eyes closed, without speaking. Nobody dared interrupt the moment.

On Sunday 4 May, Radu and Lucia invited everyone to dinner in their little flat in La Duchère, for their first wedding anniversary. Lucia made a paella so big they had to borrow the pan from the restaurant downstairs. Radu took out Hélène’s letter, the one he had read on the eve of his wedding, and read it aloud again, for everyone. Odile listened with her eyes closed, nodding at every sentence.

The following Saturday, 10 May, Odile fell in her kitchen. She got up to boil some water, felt dizzy and found herself on the floor, unable to get up. She stayed there almost an hour, unable to reach the phone. It was Rose-Hélène who raised the alarm. She was surprised not to see Odile’s door open for the morning harmonica.

Ioana used the spare key. She found Odile on the floor, conscious, pale, trying to joke. “Don’t worry,” she murmured. “I just sat down a bit too low.” Dr Martin arrived in ten minutes. He listened to her breathing for a long time, then called an ambulance. Pneumonia. She had to be admitted to hospital.

Isabelle took the first train from Paris. She spent the night at the Croix-Rousse hospital, on a chair, next to her mother’s bed. The next day she called her estate agent and announced she was bringing her move forward. She wouldn’t come in July. She would come straight away. She blamed herself for having waited so long.

Dr Martin came to see her on the third day, after his surgery hours. He sat on the edge of the bed, like an old friend rather than a doctor. They looked at each other for a long time, two doctors who both knew how to read an X-ray. “Don’t tell me stories, Martin,” Odile said. “I know how it’s done.” He smiled sadly. “Then you know you can get through this. If you rest. For once.”

The first days were hard. Odile had a fever, breathed badly, slept a lot. She had a drip in her arm and an oxygen tube under her nose, which she tried to pull out as soon as the nurse’s back was turned. “I’m fed up with this pipe,” she said. “I’m not a deep-sea diver.” The nurse, a patient young woman, put it back every time with a smile.

Julien came every afternoon, with Henri-Ion in the baby carrier. He brought flowers, newspapers, news of the lime trees. On 15 May, Odile felt better. She talked longer. And at one point, in the middle of a sentence, she called him “tu” for the first time in five years. Julien didn’t dare comment. He just felt something tighten in his chest.

She told him she wasn’t going just yet, that she still had things to do. She wanted to see the last two lime trees planted, the one in Paris and the one in Corsica. She cared about that. Julien promised to organise both plantings as soon as possible. Amina, told by phone, had already opened a new spreadsheet before he had even finished his sentence.

Visitors came one after another all week. Mrs Roux came by taxi, with her own wheelchair, and the two old ladies spent an hour comparing their wheelchairs, their medicines and their doctors, with a black humour that made the whole ward staff laugh. Mr Fournier brought a lime branch in a vase. Théo played the guitar in the corridor.

On Wednesday, the La Duchère children recorded a video for her. You could see all sixty of them, in the Hélène Morel hall, under the roof window, playing the waltz. At the third verse they all stopped together, left eight bars of silence, then went on. At the end, Inès came up to the camera and said: “The silence is your place, Madame. We’re keeping it for you. Come back soon.”

Odile watched the video three times in a row on Isabelle’s tablet. The third time, she whistled into the silence. Faintly, with the oxygen tube under her nose, but she whistled the eight bars to the end. The nurse, passing in the corridor, stopped at the door to listen. She didn’t dare come in.

Yves Le Goff sent a postcard from Nantes, with a lighthouse on it. He told her about his own stay in hospital the previous winter, and the soup, and the nurses who woke everyone at six. “I got used to it, and I got over it,” he wrote. “You’ll get over it too. Don’t go before me. I still have a crêpe for you to taste.”

Odile laughed as she read the card. Then she put it on her bedside table, next to the lime branch, Rose-Hélène’s drawing and the photo of Henri as a sailor that Isabelle had brought from the Hélène Morel hall. “Look,” she said to her daughter. “My bedside table looks like a museum. All it needs is a guard.”

Rose-Hélène hadn’t been allowed to visit the hospital in the first days, because of germs. She complained about it to everyone, with great conviction. On 18 May the doctor finally gave his permission. She came into the room with her harmonica, very solemn, and asked Odile if she had taken her medicine, exactly as the nurse did.

Odile answered yes, very obediently. So Rose-Hélène sat on the edge of the bed and played the three notes. Then she whistled the first verse, out of tune and very breathy, as on the morning of 3 May. Odile listened, smiling. When the little one had finished, she told her: “You know, you already whistle better than I did at your age. At three, all I could do was shout.”

On 25 May Odile came home. She was weaker than before, and thinner too. She could no longer go down the stairs. A nurse would come twice a day. Isabelle, who had signed the lease on her flat in rue des Fantasques, would sleep at her mother’s until she moved in. And Julien and Ioana had decided to leave their door open, permanently, across the landing.

Isabelle moved the following week, with the help of Radu, Karim and a van hired for the day. She kept only the essentials: her books, her two cats, and Henri’s sea chest, empty now, which she placed at the foot of her bed. From the windows of her new flat you could see the Rhône. From her mother’s, you could see Fourvière. “That way,” she said, “we have the whole city between the two of us.”

The first evening, Odile asked to be settled in her armchair by the window, from where she could see the roofs of the Croix-Rousse. She looked at the sky for a long time as it turned pink above the hill of Fourvière. “I’ll never tire of this view,” she said. “Forty years I’ve been looking at it, and I still can’t believe it’s mine.”

Meanwhile, Amina had been working. In three days she had obtained two planting dates everyone thought impossible. The Paris lime tree would be planted on Saturday 14 June, in front of a music school in the 19th arrondissement, next to the Philharmonie. The Corsican one on Saturday 21 June, the day of the Fête de la musique, in a little mountain village above Corte.

The last four lime trees of the partner cities, in Bordeaux, Rennes, Nice and Dijon, had been planted in May, at weekends, while Odile was in hospital. Julien had gone alone, with Amina, every other Saturday, always coming home the same evening. Each time, Odile whistled the third verse from her bed, on the tablet, with the oxygen tube under her nose. The nurses got into the habit of coming to listen.

Why a village above Corte? Because that was where Julien and Ioana, on their honeymoon four years earlier, had got lost in the mountains and met Antoine, the old shepherd who had known Julien’s grandfather. Antoine was now ninety-four. When Amina called him, he agreed straight away. “A Lyon tree in Corsica?” he said. “It’ll get used to it. People from Lyon always do.”

Odile obviously couldn’t go to Paris or to Corsica. She knew it. She didn’t complain. “I’ll watch everything on the tablet,” she said. “Like in Strasbourg. And this time I’ll whistle from my armchair, with a view of Fourvière. It’s a better seat than any concert hall.”

On Saturday 14 June, the weather in Paris was magnificent. The lime tree was planted in a school courtyard opposite the Parc de la Villette. Olivier Marchand came, leaning on a stick as well. Catherine Dumas made a two-minute speech. And the children of the Paris orchestra, created in the spring, played the waltz, leaving eight bars of silence at the third verse.

On rue d’Austerlitz, in her armchair, Odile whistled. Her voice was weak, but the tablet’s speaker carried it all the way to Paris. The children listened in silence to the old lady from Lyon whistling for them. At the end they applauded the screen. Odile gave a little wave, like a queen on a balcony.

The same day, at La Duchère, the little lime tree in front of the Hélène Morel hall flowered for the third time. Lucia sent Julien a photo, which he showed to Odile. She looked at the little yellow flowers for a long time. “Two years,” she said. “It flowered for the first time six weeks after Hélène died. It always flowers in June. It has never forgotten.”

On Saturday 21 June, in Corsica, the planting was the strangest and most beautiful of all. The village had forty inhabitants. They were all there, in the little square in front of the church. Antoine, sitting on a straw chair, held the lime tree on his lap, as Odile had on the train to Marseille. Julien and Ioana had come with both children. It was Henri-Ion’s first trip.

There was no orchestra in the village. But there was an old shepherd who played the cetera, a kind of Corsican mandolin, and three women who sang in polyphony. They had learned the waltz by listening to Henri’s recording, the one from Dakar, which Julien had sent them. They had arranged it in their own way, with deep voices and chords that smelled of the maquis.

On the tablet, propped on the church wall, Odile was listening from Lyon. When the three women reached the third verse, they fell silent. And in the silence of the mountain, eight hundred kilometres away, you could hear an old lady whistling, faintly, carefully, the eight bars that belonged to her.

Antoine planted the lime tree himself, with his shepherd’s hands, without a shovel. Then he turned to the tablet and spoke to Odile, in French, with his Corsican accent. “Madame,” he said, “your tree has arrived. It’s home now. Here we keep trees a very long time. Longer than people. It’ll still be here in two hundred years.”

In the evening, Julien called Odile from the village square, while the villagers were preparing a meal under the chestnut trees. He told her everything she hadn’t been able to see: the cetera, the women’s voices, Antoine’s hands in the earth. She listened without interrupting. Then she said, in a very calm voice: “Twelve lime trees. All planted. I can go in peace now.”

Julien felt his heart stop. “Don’t say that, Odile.” She laughed softly at the other end of the line. “Don’t worry, my dear. I wasn’t talking about leaving today. I was just saying I’ve done what I had to do. It’s not the same thing. And besides, I still have a crêpe to taste in Nantes. I have no right to disappoint a Breton sailor.”

Ioana, sitting beside Julien on a stone bench, took his hand. She had heard the whole conversation. She said nothing. She was watching Rose-Hélène running round the square with the village children, harmonica in hand, and Henri-Ion, asleep in the arms of an old Corsican woman who was singing him a lullaby in a language he would never understand.

That evening, in the little stone house where they were sleeping, above the village, Ioana found Julien sitting at the open window, his notebook on his knees. He wasn’t writing. He was looking at the stars above the mountain, so many that they looked like dust. She sat down beside him. “Are you afraid?” she asked.

Julien took a long time to answer. “Yes,” he said at last. “I’m afraid. Not for her. She’s afraid of nothing. I’m afraid for us. I don’t know how we’ll manage without her, across the landing.” Ioana rested her head on his shoulder. “We’ll do what she did for Henri,” she answered. “We’ll whistle.”

They stayed at the window a long time, without speaking, listening to the crickets and the wind in the chestnut trees. Then, very softly, Julien whistled the first three notes of the waltz towards the mountain. He knew that eight hundred kilometres away, on rue d’Austerlitz, an old lady was asleep in her armchair, facing Fourvière. He didn’t know that she had woken at that very moment, and smiled.

Yves Le Goff sends Odile a postcard at the hospital. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Dear Odile, Julien told me you were in hospital. Don’t worry: sea folk always pull through. Henri used to say you were sturdier than a cargo ship.
I spent a month in hospital last winter too. I was fed up with the soup and with the nurses who woke me at six. But I got used to it, and I got over it. You’ll get over it too.

I blame myself a little, you know. For fifty-three years I kept that cassette in a drawer. I should have sent it to you sooner. But I didn’t dare. I thought Henri would still hold it against me, even from up there.
Julien told me little Henri-Ion smiled when he heard the harmonica. I can’t believe it. A four-month-old baby recognising the music of a sailor who died eight years ago. Henri would have laughed.

I received Amina’s invitation for the Lyon planting next spring. I care about it a lot. If my legs still carry me, I’ll come. And we’ll whistle the waltz together, you and I, as on the deck of the cargo ship.
So hold on. Don’t go before me. I still have a crêpe for you to taste, without cassava this time. With all my friendship, Yves.
